story: In the constellation Corona Borealis sits a bizarre, dying supergiant that repeatedly vanishes from the night sky. Discovered by astronomer Edward Pigott in 1795, R Coronae Borealis normally glows right at the threshold of naked-eye visibility at magnitude six. But without warning, it abruptly drops by up to nine magnitudes, plunging into complete invisibility. Astronomers call it a reverse nova. Unlike a standard nova that explodes in brilliance, this star chokes itself. Because its atmosphere is nearly devoid of hydrogen and packed with helium and carbon, expanding gas cools until carbon rapidly condenses into microscopic soot grains. A puff of carbon dust weighing no more than an asteroid drifts directly into our line of sight, blotting out the star's optical light by thousands of times. Its total energy output never drops; it simply hides behind its own smoke until radiation pressure slowly sweeps the dust away.
angle: A supergiant star repeatedly chokes itself into complete invisibility by puffing out clouds of cosmic soot directly into our line of sight.
disputed: The formation channel of R Coronae Borealis: [S5] argues isotopic evidence strongly favors a white dwarf merger, whereas [S6] asserts evidence points to a post-AGB helium flash, while [S1], [S3], and [S7] treat both as viable competing models. The script should attribute this as an active scientific debate: 'Astronomers still debate whether it formed from the violent collision of two white dwarfs or a dying star's final helium flash.'

The exact location of carbon dust condensation: [S2] highlights two contrasting models—one where dust condenses at 20 stellar radii where temperatures reach 1,500 K, and another where condensation happens directly in atmospheric shock fronts within the photosphere. The script should describe the process generally without asserting an exact distance from the star.
